title: Heat and temperature: how a thermometer works, and why hot things cool down

summary.text: Leave a tumbler of hot water and a tumbler of cold water on the same table, and the hot one cools while the cold one warms. Both stop at the temperature of the room. Temperature is how hot or cold something is, and a thermometer measures it in degrees Celsius. Heat always moves by itself from a warmer thing to a cooler one, until both are equally warm. A cold thing is a thing with less heat, and no cold flows anywhere.
summary.art: Two steel tumblers side by side on a wooden table, one with a wisp of steam and one with drops of water on the outside, a red-liquid thermometer standing in each, and arrows showing heat leaving the hot one and entering the cold one.

intro.hook: Put one hand in a bowl of warm water and the other in a bowl of ice water for one minute. Then put both hands into one bowl of tap water. One hand says the water is warm. The other hand says it is cold. Which hand is right?
intro.text: Neither hand is right, because your skin compares the water with how warm it was a moment ago. To know how hot something really is, we need a thermometer. In this unit you learn to read one. You watch hot water and cold water change, minute by minute, and find out where they stop. You make a thermometer from a bottle and a straw. And you find out what really moves when a hot thing cools down.
intro.art: Three steel bowls in a row on a kitchen counter: warm water with a little steam on the left, ice cubes on the right, and plain tap water in the middle, with a child's two hands about to go into the middle bowl.

outcomes: I can read a thermometer in degrees Celsius, and I wait until the reading stops changing.
I can explain why my hand is not a good way to measure temperature, using the two-hands bowl test.
I can explain how a liquid thermometer works: the liquid expands when it warms and climbs up a narrow tube.
I can say which way heat moves between two things that touch, and predict that they end up at the same temperature.
I can explain, using my own readings, why a hot tumbler and a cold tumbler both end up at room temperature.
I can tell heat and temperature apart: a small cup can be hotter than a big pot, but hold less heat.
I can tell how Pictet's snow seemed to send out cold, and how Prévost showed that only heat was moving.

explanations.definition: Temperature is how hot or cold something is. In India we measure it in degrees Celsius, written °C.
explanations.description: On the Celsius scale, 0 is the temperature at which pure water freezes. 100 is the temperature at which it boils, at sea level. The space between them is cut into 100 equal steps called degrees. Anything colder than freezing water gets a minus number. A freezer is about minus 18 °C. The scale is named after Anders Celsius, a Swedish astronomer. In 1742 he made a scale with 100 for freezing and 0 for boiling. A few years later, others turned it the other way round, which is how we use it today.
examples: A fridge is about 4 °C inside.
A healthy body is about 37 °C inside.
Tea people drink is often about 60 to 65 °C.
explanations.art: A tall thermometer with labels beside it: a freezer at minus 18, ice at 0, a fridge at 4, a room at 30, a child at 37, tea at 60, boiling water at 100.
explanations.context: This card explains what a temperature number means.

explanations.definition: A liquid thermometer has a bulb of liquid joined to a very narrow tube. When the liquid warms, it expands and climbs up the tube. When it cools, it shrinks and goes down.
explanations.description: The liquid expands only a tiny bit. But the tube is so narrow that this tiny bit of extra liquid makes a long line. The numbers on the side were marked by putting the thermometer in melting ice and in boiling water. A thermometer shows its own temperature. Put it in hot water, and heat moves into the bulb until the bulb is as warm as the water. That takes about a minute for a glass thermometer. So you wait until the line stops moving before you read it. Most laboratory thermometers in India use red-coloured spirit. Old ones used silvery mercury, which is poisonous if the glass breaks.
examples: Dip the bulb in hot water and the red line climbs for about a minute, then stops.
A digital thermometer has a tiny metal part instead of liquid, and it shows a number on a screen.
If you read too early, the number is too low for hot water and too high for cold water.
explanations.art: A thermometer bulb in hot water, with a zoomed-in picture of the narrow tube and the red liquid creeping up it.
explanations.context: This card explains why the red line moves, and why you must wait before reading it.

explanations.definition: A clinical thermometer is made for bodies and reads only from about 32 to 42 °C. A laboratory thermometer reads a much wider range, usually from about minus 10 to 110 °C.
explanations.description: A body's temperature changes only a little, so a clinical thermometer has a short range with small, exact steps. Most digital fever thermometers show 'Lo' or 'Hi' outside their range. That is why a fever thermometer cannot measure fridge water or hot tea. A laboratory thermometer is long and has a wide range, so it can measure ice, a room and hot water. But it must never go in the mouth, and it is not made for fevers.
examples: A fever thermometer in fridge water shows 'Lo'.
A laboratory thermometer in the same water might show 8 °C.
A glass clinical thermometer has a small kink in its tube, so the line stays put after you take it out.
explanations.art: A short white digital fever thermometer and a long glass laboratory thermometer lying side by side, with their ranges written underneath.
explanations.context: This card explains why a fever thermometer will not work for the experiments in this unit.

explanations.concept: Heat moves from warmer to cooler
explanations.definition: When two things at different temperatures touch, heat moves from the warmer one to the cooler one. It keeps moving until both are at the same temperature.
explanations.description: Hot water on a table gives heat to the air and the table, so it cools. Cold water on the same table takes heat from the air, so it warms. Both stop changing when they reach room temperature. Then there is no difference left, and no more heat moves either way. This always happens by itself. Heat never moves by itself from a cooler thing to a warmer one. A fridge makes its inside cold by pumping heat out, and that is why the back of a fridge feels warm.
examples: Curd taken out of the fridge warms up on the table.
A hot idli steamer cools down after the stove is turned off.
Drops form on the outside of a tumbler of cold water, because the cold tumbler cools the damp air next to it.
explanations.art: A table with a hot tumbler and a cold tumbler, red arrows going out of the hot one into the air and from the air into the cold one, and a thermometer on the wall.
explanations.context: This card explains the hot and cold tumbler test: why both tumblers end up at room temperature.

explanations.definition: Cold is not a separate thing that moves. A cold thing has less heat than a warm thing.
explanations.description: People say 'Shut the door, the cold is coming in.' What really happens is that heat from the warm room is going out. When you hold an ice cube, the ice does not send cold into your hand. Your hand sends heat into the ice. Your hand cools down because it is losing heat, and the ice melts because it is gaining heat. Scientists in the 1790s argued about this, and the idea that only heat moves won.
examples: Ice in your hand melts because your hand's heat goes into it.
A room gets cold on a winter night because its heat leaks out through windows and walls.
A steel tumbler of fridge water feels cold because heat is leaving your fingers.
explanations.art: A child holding an ice cube, with red arrows going from the palm into the ice, and a drop running down the wrist.
explanations.context: This card explains why there is no such thing as cold flowing into something.

explanations.concept: What heat really is: jiggling particles
explanations.definition: Everything is made of tiny particles that are always jiggling. The hotter a thing is, the faster its particles jiggle. Temperature tells us how fast they jiggle, on average.
explanations.description: When hot water touches a cooler tumbler, the fast-jiggling water particles bump into the slower tumbler particles. Each bump passes on a little movement. So the tumbler's particles speed up, and the water's particles slow down. That passing-on of movement is heat moving. When both jiggle equally fast, the bumps pass on as much one way as the other, so the temperatures stay the same. Scientists showed in the 1800s that heat is this movement, and not a hidden fluid inside things.
examples: Sugar dissolves faster in hot water, because the fast water particles knock the sugar particles apart sooner.
Rubbing your palms makes their particles jiggle faster, so they get warm.
The smell of hot sambar spreads faster than the smell of cold curd.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in circle where a hot water particle with long wiggle lines bumps a steel particle with short wiggle lines, and the steel particle starts to wiggle more.
explanations.context: This card explains what is happening inside a thing when it gets hotter, and when heat moves.

explanations.concept: Heat and temperature are not the same
explanations.definition: Temperature is how hot a thing is. Heat is the energy it can give to something cooler. A big amount of warm water can hold more heat than a small cup of hotter water.
explanations.description: Fill a small katori with water at 70 °C, and a big bucket with water at 40 °C. The katori is hotter. But put the same lump of ice in each, and the bucket melts much more ice, because it has so much more water to give heat. Temperature does not tell you how much heat a thing holds. It only tells you how hot it is, and so which way heat will move.
examples: A drop of hot tea that splashes on your hand stings, but cools in a moment. A cupful would burn.
A big pot of sambar stays hot for much longer than a small bowl of it.
The sea in Chennai or Kochi warms up and cools down far more slowly than the sand.
explanations.art: A small katori of hot water with a big ice cube still mostly there, next to a big bucket of warm water where the same ice cube has melted away.
explanations.context: This card explains why 'hot' and 'a lot of heat' are different.

explanations.concept: Why your hand is not a thermometer
explanations.definition: Your skin feels whether it is warming up or cooling down. So the same water can feel warm to one hand and cold to the other.
explanations.description: In the two-hands bowl test, one hand had been in warm water, so it was warm. In the middle bowl it lost heat, and it felt cold. The other hand had been in ice water, so it was cold. In the middle bowl it gained heat, and it felt warm. The water was one temperature all along, and a thermometer showed one number. The English thinker John Locke wrote about this same test, with one warm hand and one cold hand in the same water, in 1690.
examples: After a cold bath, ordinary tap water feels warm.
Coming out of an air-conditioned shop, the street feels even hotter than it is.
A parent's hand on a child's forehead can tell 'hot' or 'not hot', but not 38.5 or 39.5.
explanations.art: Two hands in the same middle bowl, one with a little blue 'cold?' bubble and one with a little red 'warm?' bubble, and a thermometer in the bowl showing one number.
explanations.context: This card explains the two-hands bowl test, and why we need a thermometer.

agreed.text: Heat moves by itself from a warmer thing to a cooler thing, and never the other way.
agreed.evidence: Every time anyone measures it, hot things in a room cool down and cold things warm up, until they reach the same temperature. Scientists call this the second law of thermodynamics.

agreed.text: Things that touch for long enough end up at the same temperature.
agreed.evidence: A thermometer shows that a tumbler of hot water and a tumbler of cold water left in a room both reach room temperature within a few hours.

agreed.text: Temperature is how fast the particles of a thing jiggle, on average.
agreed.evidence: In the 1800s, scientists such as James Joule showed that stirring or rubbing always makes the same amount of heat for the same amount of work. Later, Albert Einstein and Jean Perrin showed that the tiny particles really are always moving.

agreed.text: Most liquids, solids and gases expand when they warm up.
agreed.evidence: This is how liquid thermometers work. It is also why railway tracks and bridges are built with small gaps, so they have room to expand on hot days.

challenging.claim: Cold is a thing that flows into warm things, like through an open door.
challenging.who: A very common idea, which some scientists also held in the 1790s
challenging.for: When you open a door on a winter night, the room feels as if cold is pouring in. Pictet's snow even seemed to send out cold through mirrors.
challenging.against: A thermometer shows heat leaving warm things, never cold arriving. Prévost explained Pictet's snow: the thermometer gave out more heat than it got back from the snow.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that cold is something that moves.

challenging.claim: Heat is an invisible fluid, called caloric, stored inside things.
challenging.for: Heat seemed to flow from hot to cold like water running downhill, and a warm thing seemed to hold a certain amount of it.
challenging.against: Rubbing, stirring and drilling can make heat for as long as you keep going. A stored fluid would run out. So heat is a kind of movement of particles.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of what heat is.

challenging.claim: A thermometer shows the right temperature as soon as it touches something.
challenging.who: A common mistake when people first use a thermometer
challenging.for: A digital thermometer shows a number at once, so it seems ready.
challenging.against: The thermometer shows its own temperature. Heat takes time to move in or out of it, so the number keeps changing for a while. You must wait until it stops.
challenging.context: This card is about reading a thermometer too quickly.

challenging.claim: Hot water can freeze faster than cold water.
challenging.who: Erasto Mpemba, a schoolboy in Tanzania, who noticed it while making ice cream in 1963. He wrote about it with the physicist Denis Osborne in 1969.
challenging.for: Some careful experiments have found hot water freezing first, perhaps because it loses water by evaporating, or because of how it moves as it cools.
challenging.against: Other careful experiments do not find it at all. The result seems to depend on the container, the freezer and exactly how 'frozen' is measured.
challenging.context: This card is about a real puzzle that scientists still argue about.

big_questions.q: Your hot tumbler gave its heat to the room. Where is that heat now?
big_questions.hint: Think about the air, the table and the walls. Did the room get warmer? Why was it too little to notice?

big_questions.q: If heat always spreads from warmer to cooler, will everything in the world one day be the same temperature?
big_questions.hint: Think about what keeps making new warm places, like the Sun and your own body.

big_questions.q: A thermometer tells you its own temperature. How do you know it is telling you the water's temperature too?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens when two things touch for a while.

big_questions.q: Is there a coldest possible temperature? What would happen to the particles there?
big_questions.hint: If temperature is how fast particles jiggle, what is the slowest they could go?

big_questions.q: Your hand and a thermometer said different things about the same water. Which one tells the truth about the world?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each one is really measuring. Is a feeling of warmth wrong, or is it about something else?

story.title: Where Did Paati's Coffee Go?
story.note: The story is made up. The science is true: hot coffee in a room cools to room temperature, a tumbler standing in water gives its heat to the water until both meet in the middle, and pouring coffee between a tumbler and a davara cools it faster.
text: Every morning in Kumbakonam, Paati made filter coffee. She poured it from the steel tumbler into the wide davara and back again, high in the air, until it was frothy. Then she put the tumbler on the window sill and went to bathe.

Lakshmi was nine, and her aunt Revathi Athai was a science teacher. Athai had lent Lakshmi a long glass thermometer for the holidays. It had red liquid inside and numbers from minus 10 to 110 along the side. Lakshmi had already measured the fridge, the tap water and the air on the balcony.
That morning she dipped the bulb of the thermometer into Paati's coffee. The red line climbed and climbed, then stopped. "Seventy degrees," she read.
Her cousin Arjun, who was seven, looked over her shoulder. "That is very hot," he said.
Lakshmi wrote 70 in her notebook. Then she measured the air in the room. The line slid down to 29. She wrote that too.
When Paati came back from her bath, the coffee had gone lukewarm. Lakshmi measured it again. "Forty-two," she said. "It went down by 28 degrees."
"Of course it went down," said Paati, drinking it anyway. "Coffee always goes cold if you leave it."
Lakshmi frowned. "But where did the heat go, Paati? The coffee had lots of heat, and now it has less. Heat must go somewhere."
"It just disappears," said Arjun. "Like steam."
Lakshmi measured the air in the room again. Still 29. "The room did not get hotter," she said. "So maybe Arjun is right. Maybe heat just vanishes."
But she was not happy with that answer. That evening she phoned Revathi Athai.
"Try this," said Athai. "Stand a tumbler of hot water inside a bigger vessel of ordinary water. Then measure both, again and again."

The next morning, Paati made extra coffee. Lakshmi poured one tumbler of it and stood it inside Paati's big steel vessel. Arjun poured tap water into the vessel, all around the tumbler, until the water came most of the way up the side. Lakshmi measured the coffee. Seventy. She measured the water around it. Twenty-nine, the same as the room.
Every two minutes, Lakshmi stirred the water in the vessel gently with a spoon. Then she measured the coffee, and then the water, and Arjun wrote the numbers down.
The coffee went down. 62. 55. 49. 45.
And the water around it went up. 31. 33. 35. 36.
"Look!" said Arjun. "The water is getting hotter. And nobody is heating it."
"The coffee is heating it," said Lakshmi slowly. "The heat is going out of the coffee, through the steel, into the water. It did not disappear. It moved."
After twenty minutes, the coffee read 39 and the water read 38. After half an hour, both read 38. Then the numbers stopped changing.
"They met in the middle," said Arjun.
"Not quite the middle," said Lakshmi. "There is much more water than coffee. So the coffee came down a long way, and the water went up only a little."

Then she sat very still. "That is what happened yesterday too," she said. "The coffee gave its heat to the air in the room. But the room has so much air that it warmed up too little for the thermometer to show."
Paati had been listening from the kitchen. "So when I pour the coffee between the tumbler and the davara," she said, "am I giving its heat to the air?"
Lakshmi thought about it. "Yes, Paati. When you pour it high, lots of coffee touches the air at once. The heat leaves faster, so the coffee cools down enough to drink."
"Then tomorrow," said Paati, "I will pour it only twice, and you two can drink it hot."
Arjun tapped the notebook. "I still don't understand one thing," he said. "If the coffee gives heat to the water, why doesn't the water give cold to the coffee?"

Lakshmi smiled, because she had asked Athai the same question. "There is no such thing as giving cold," she said. "Cold just means less heat. The heat only ever goes one way, from the hotter thing to the cooler thing. It stops when they are the same."
That night, Lakshmi wrote at the bottom of her page: The heat did not vanish. It spread out.
story.epiphany: For the parent: when a hot thing cools, its heat does not vanish. It moves into whatever is cooler around it: the air, the table, the water. In a big room the air gets only a tiny bit warmer, too little to measure, so the heat seems to disappear. A vessel of water is small enough to show the rise. The coffee and the water stopped at the same temperature, nearer the water's starting temperature, because there was more water. Heat moves only from hotter to cooler, and stops when they are equal. Cold is not a thing that moves.
ask: Why did the room still read 29 degrees after the coffee had cooled?
In the vessel test, what happened to the water around the tumbler? Why?
Why did the coffee and the water end up nearer 29 than 70?
Why does Paati's high pouring cool the coffee faster?
Arjun asked why the water did not give cold to the coffee. How would you answer him?

rules: Shuffle the temperature cards and lay them number side down.
On your turn, turn over the top two cards with the words showing, not the number.
Say which one you think is hotter, and why.
Then say which way the heat would go if the two things touched.
Turn the cards over to check the numbers. A right 'hotter' guess scores 1 point, and a right heat direction scores 1 more.
Every third turn, take a question card instead.
After everyone has had 6 turns, lay all the cards in one long line from coldest to hottest.

check.q: Hot coffee spills into a warm bath. Which way does the heat move?
options: From the bath into the coffee, because the bath is bigger
From the coffee into the bath water, because the coffee is hotter
No heat moves, because both are warm
check.why: Heat moves from the hotter thing to the cooler thing. The coffee is about 65 °C and the bath is about 40 °C, so heat goes from the coffee into the bath. The bath is bigger, so it holds more heat. But the direction depends on temperature, not size.

flow.kid: Turn two cards. Which is hotter? Which way would the heat go?
flow.parent: The surprises children enjoy most: a hen is warmer than a person, a pressure cooker is hotter than boiling water, and the Moon's dark craters are far colder than any freezer.

flow.kid: Make one long line, coldest to hottest. Where do you go?

check.q: Which of these is the hottest?
options: Inside your body
A child with a fever
A hen's body
check.why: A hen's body is about 41 °C, warmer than a person with a fever. Birds run warmer than people. Picking the fever is a good guess, because a fever is hotter than usual for a person. But it is about 39 °C.

experiments.title: Hot Tumbler, Cold Tumbler: where do they both end up?
experiments.question: If a tumbler of hot water and a tumbler of cold water stand on the same table, what happens to each one's temperature, and where does it stop?
experiments.predict: Guess the temperature of each tumbler after 20 minutes, and again after 3 hours. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two tumblers of the same size and metal, filled to the same height. Stand them side by side, away from the fan, the sun and the stove. Use the same thermometer for every reading, and read both tumblers at the same times. Stir gently and wait until the line stops moving before reading, because a thermometer takes about a minute to catch up.

materials.item: a laboratory thermometer that reads from about minus 10 to 110 °C, or a digital kitchen probe thermometer. A fever thermometer will not work, because it reads only from about 32 to 42 °C.
two steel tumblers of the same size
hot water: half boiled water and half tap water, mixed by a grown-up. It should be about as hot as tea for drinking.
cold water from a bottle in the fridge. No fridge? Tap water with four ice cubes, with the ice taken out after five minutes.
a spoon for stirring, a cloth to wipe the thermometer, a clock or phone timer
a notebook and pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the water, mixes it and pours it. The child does not touch the hot tumbler. Glass thermometers break easily: hold them by the top, never stir with them, and lay them flat on a cloth so they cannot roll off the table.

schedule.what: Read the room. Set up a hot and a cold tumbler. Read both every 5 minutes for 20 minutes.
Three hours later, read both tumblers and the room again.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw two lines on one graph, one for each tumbler, with time along the bottom. Draw a dotted line across for the room.
experiments.context: In this experiment you watch a hot tumbler and a cold tumbler on the same table, and measure where each one ends up.

setup.art: A child holding a red-liquid thermometer in the air in a shady corner of a room, looking at the numbers.
setup.caption: 1. Measure the air in the room.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers side by side on a table, one with a little steam rising, a thermometer standing in it.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up fills one tumbler with hot water and one with cold.

setup.art: A notebook with a table of times and numbers, a phone timer showing 5 minutes, and two tumblers behind it.
setup.caption: 3. Read both every 5 minutes. Then again after 3 hours.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the numbers on the thermometer. 2. Hold it by the top, in the air, in a shady place. 3. Wait 2 minutes, then read where the red line ends. 4. Write it as the room temperature.
flow.say: This is a thermometer. The red line climbs when it gets warmer. First let's measure the air in this room. We wait until the line stops moving.
flow.kid: Hold the thermometer in the air. Wait 2 minutes. Where does the red line stop? Write that number.
flow.parent: Most homes in South India read between about 26 and 32 degrees. Show your child how to read the line at eye level. If the line is between two marks, choose the nearer one. A digital probe just shows the number, but still wait until it stops changing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hot Tumbler, Cold Tumbler test. Here you learn to read the thermometer by measuring the air in the room.

flow.do: 1. Show the two empty tumblers. 2. Explain that one will hold hot water and one cold water. 3. Ask for a guess for each tumbler, after 20 minutes and after 3 hours, with a reason. 4. Write the guesses.
flow.say: One tumbler will be hot and one will be cold. What will each one read after 20 minutes? And after 3 hours? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One tumbler hot, one tumbler cold. Guess each number after 20 minutes. Then after 3 hours. Why?

ask.q: Will the cold tumbler stay cold?
good: It will warm up, because the room is warmer.
It will get closer to the room's number.

flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. Many children think the hot water will cool right down to cold, or that the cold one will stay cold. Any guess with a reason is good.

flow.do: 1. Boil some water. 2. Mix it half and half with tap water in a jug. 3. Fill one tumbler to about 2 cm below the rim. 4. Fill the other with fridge water to the same height. 5. Stand them a hand apart on the table, away from the fan.
flow.say: I am making the hot water now, because it can burn. I am filling both tumblers to the same height. Why should they be the same?
flow.kid: A grown-up pours the hot water. Do not touch that tumbler. Why fill both the same?
flow.parent: Half boiled and half tap water should be about 60 to 65 degrees, which is hot but not scalding. Keep the fan off if you can, or keep it the same all the time, because moving air cools things faster.

flow.do: 1. Stand the thermometer in the hot tumbler, stir gently with a spoon, and wait until the line stops. 2. Read it and write it. 3. Wipe the thermometer, and do the same with the cold tumbler. 4. Repeat every 5 minutes, at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes.
flow.say: Let's read both tumblers now, and then every 5 minutes. Read the hot one first, then the cold one. What do you notice about the numbers?
flow.kid: Read the hot tumbler. Then the cold one. Write both numbers. Do it again every 5 minutes.
flow.parent: Each reading takes about a minute, so a 5-minute gap gives time for both. A typical result with a 30 degree room: the hot tumbler goes 62, 56, 52, 48, 45. The cold one goes 8, 11, 13, 15, 16. Notice that the hot one falls fastest at the start, when it is furthest from the room. Drops of water may appear on the outside of the cold tumbler. They come from the damp air next to it, not from inside.

check.q: The cold tumbler's number went up. Where did its heat come from?
options: From the hot tumbler, through the thermometer
From the air and the table around it, which were warmer
Cold water makes its own heat
check.why: The air and the table were at room temperature, warmer than the fridge water. So heat moved from them into the cold water. Picking the hot tumbler is a good thought, because heat does go from hot to cold. But the tumblers do not touch, and the thermometer was wiped and moved, so very little could pass that way.

flow.do: 1. Leave both tumblers where they are. 2. After 3 hours, read both and the room. 3. Write the three numbers.
flow.say: Three hours have gone by. Let's read both tumblers and the room. Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Three hours later. Read both tumblers. Read the room. Are they close?
flow.parent: Both tumblers should now read within a degree or two of the room. The tumbler that started hot may even read a degree below the room, because water evaporating from its top cools it a little. That is real, not a mistake.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: hot things and cold things in a room both end up at room temperature. What I saw: the hot tumbler went down from 62 to 31, and the cold one went up from 8 to 29. The room was 30. Why: heat moves from the warmer thing to the cooler thing until they are the same.

check.q: After 3 hours, why did both tumblers stop changing?
options: The water got tired
They were both at room temperature, so there was no difference left to make heat move
The thermometer stopped working
check.why: Heat moves only when there is a difference in temperature. Once both tumblers were as warm as the room, heat stopped moving in or out. Picking 'the thermometer stopped working' is a fair worry. You can check by dipping it in warm water, and it moves again.

experiments.title: Tumbler in a Bowl: where does the heat go?
experiments.question: When a hot tumbler stands in a bowl of room-temperature water, what happens to the tumbler and to the water around it?
experiments.predict: Will the water in the bowl get warmer, colder or stay the same? Where will the two numbers stop? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Read the tumbler and the bowl at the same times, every 2 minutes. Stir the bowl water gently before each reading, so the warm water near the tumbler mixes in. Do not move the tumbler.

materials.item: a laboratory thermometer that reads from about minus 10 to 110 °C, or a digital kitchen probe thermometer. A fever thermometer will not work, because it reads only from about 32 to 42 °C.
a steel tumbler
a big steel vessel or bowl that the tumbler fits inside, with room around it
hot water, half boiled and half tap water, mixed by a grown-up
tap water at room temperature, about three tumblers full
a spoon, a cloth, a timer, a notebook and pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water and lowers the tumbler into the bowl. The child stirs only the outer water, with a spoon.

schedule.what: Stand a hot tumbler in a bowl of room water. Read both every 2 minutes until they match.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw both lines on one graph and circle the place where they meet.
experiments.context: In this experiment a hot tumbler stands in a bowl of water, so you can see where its heat goes.

setup.art: A steel tumbler of steaming water standing inside a wide steel vessel of water, the water coming two thirds of the way up the tumbler.
setup.caption: 1. Stand a hot tumbler in a bowl of room water.

setup.art: A child stirring the outer water with a spoon while a thermometer stands in it.
setup.caption: 2. Stir the bowl. Read the bowl and the tumbler.

setup.art: A graph with one line falling and one line rising until they meet and run flat together.
setup.caption: 3. Keep reading until the two numbers meet.

flow.do: 1. Pour about three tumblers of tap water into the big bowl. 2. Read its temperature. 3. Ask your child to guess what will happen to it when a hot tumbler stands in it, and why.
flow.say: This water is the same as the room. Soon a hot tumbler will stand in the middle. Will this water change? Where will the two numbers stop?
flow.kid: A hot tumbler will stand in this water. Will the water change? Why?

ask.q: Where do you think the two numbers will stop?

flow.context: This is the first step of Tumbler in a Bowl. You guess what a hot tumbler will do to the water around it.

flow.do: 1. Mix hot water as before. 2. Fill the tumbler to the same height as the water in the bowl will reach. 3. Lower it gently into the middle of the bowl. 4. Read the tumbler at once.
flow.say: I am lowering the hot tumbler into the bowl. Watch the thermometer in it.
flow.kid: A grown-up puts the hot tumbler in the bowl. Read the tumbler.
flow.parent: If the tumbler floats or tips, pour a little water out of the bowl. The bowl water should come most of the way up the tumbler's side.

flow.do: 1. Every 2 minutes, stir the bowl water gently. 2. Read the bowl, then the tumbler. 3. Write both. 4. Stop when the two numbers are the same for two readings in a row.
flow.say: Let's read both every 2 minutes. What is happening to each number? Are they getting closer?
flow.kid: Stir the bowl. Read the bowl. Read the tumbler. Write both. Again in 2 minutes.
flow.parent: With one thermometer, wipe it and wait a moment between the two readings. A typical result: the tumbler goes 62, 54, 48, 44, 41, 39, 38. The bowl goes 30, 32, 34, 35, 36, 37, 37. They meet nearer the bowl's start, because the bowl holds more water.

check.q: The water in the bowl got warmer, though nobody heated it. Why?
options: Heat moved from the hot tumbler, through the steel, into the cooler water
Cold moved out of the bowl water into the tumbler
Stirring made it warm
check.why: Heat moves from the warmer thing to the cooler thing. The steel tumbler passed the heat from the hot water into the bowl water. Picking 'cold moved out' is how many people talk, but nothing called cold moves. Stirring does make a tiny bit of heat, far too little to show on a thermometer.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the hot tumbler's heat went into the water around it. What I saw: the tumbler went down and the bowl went up, until both read 37. Why: heat moves from hotter to cooler until they are the same. The bowl had more water, so it went up only a little.

experiments.title: Half and Half: what do you get when you mix hot and cold?
experiments.question: If you mix equal amounts of hot water and cold water, what temperature do you get?
experiments.predict: Read the hot water and the cold water first. Then guess the temperature of the mix. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Measure the same amount of hot and cold water with the same katori or measuring cup. Mix them quickly and stir. Read the mix as soon as the line stops moving.

materials.item: a laboratory thermometer that reads from about minus 10 to 110 °C, or a digital kitchen probe thermometer. A fever thermometer will not work, because it reads only from about 32 to 42 °C.
a katori or measuring cup, used for every amount
three steel tumblers
hot water, half boiled and half tap water, mixed by a grown-up
cold water from the fridge
a spoon, a cloth, a notebook and pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up measures and pours the hot water. Mix over a tray or the sink in case of spills.

schedule.what: Mix equal amounts of hot and cold water and read the mix. Then try 1 katori hot with 2 katoris cold.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Next to each try, write how far your guess was from the real mix.
experiments.context: In this experiment you mix hot and cold water and find out what temperature the mix ends up at.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers, one with steam and one with drops on the outside, each with one katori of water, and a thermometer beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Measure one katori of hot water and one of cold.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring both tumblers into a third tumbler while a child stirs.
setup.caption: 2. Pour both into one tumbler and stir.

setup.art: A thermometer in the mixed water, the red line halfway between two marks.
setup.caption: 3. Read the mix.

flow.do: 1. Pour one katori of hot water into one tumbler and one katori of cold water into another. 2. Read and write both temperatures. 3. Ask for a guess for the mix, with a reason.
flow.say: Here is one katori of hot water and one of cold. Let's read both. If we mix them, what will the mix read? Why?
flow.kid: Read the hot water. Read the cold water. Guess the mix. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Half and Half. You read hot and cold water, then guess what their mix will read.

flow.do: 1. Pour both into the third tumbler. 2. Stir for 10 seconds. 3. Read the mix and write it.
flow.say: Now I pour them together. Stir it. What does it read? How close was your guess?
flow.kid: Stir the mix. Read it. Was your guess close?
flow.parent: Equal amounts at 60 and 10 give a mix close to 35, the number exactly in the middle. It is usually a degree or two lower, because some heat goes into the tumbler and the air.

check.q: Equal amounts of water at 60 °C and 10 °C are mixed. About what will the mix read?
options: 70 °C, because the two numbers add up
About 35 °C, halfway between
10 °C, because cold wins
check.why: The hot water gives heat to the cold water until they are the same. With equal amounts, the hot water comes down as far as the cold water goes up, so they meet halfway. Adding the numbers is a common first guess, but mixing never makes water hotter than the hottest part.

flow.do: 1. Now use 1 katori of hot water and 2 katoris of cold. 2. Ask for a new guess with a reason. 3. Mix, stir and read.
flow.say: This time there is twice as much cold water. Will the mix be nearer the hot number or the cold number? Why?
flow.kid: Now 1 katori hot and 2 katoris cold. Will the mix be nearer hot or cold? Why?
flow.parent: With 60 and 10, the mix should read about 25 to 27, nearer the cold number. A good way to think: one hot katori gives its heat to share among three katoris.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: when hot and cold water mix, they meet somewhere in between. What I saw: equal amounts met near the middle, and more cold water pulled the mix nearer the cold number. Why: the hot water gives heat to the cold water, and more water needs more heat to warm up.

activities.title: The Two-Hands Bowl: can your hands measure temperature?

materials.item: three bowls, big enough for a child's hand
warm water, like a comfortable bath, from a geyser or mixed by a grown-up
ice water: tap water with a handful of ice cubes
plain tap water
a laboratory thermometer that reads from about minus 10 to 110 °C, or a digital kitchen probe thermometer. A fever thermometer will not work, because it reads only from about 32 to 42 °C.
a towel

activities.safety: A grown-up checks the warm water with their own wrist first. It must feel pleasantly warm, never hot.

schedule.what: Put one hand in warm water and one in ice water, then both in tap water. Then measure the tap water.

activities.record: Write what each hand said about the middle bowl. Then write the thermometer's number.
activities.context: This is a quick test to start the unit. Your two hands give two different answers about the same bowl of water.

setup.art: Three steel bowls in a row: steaming warm water, ice cubes in water, and plain water in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Warm on the left, ice on the right, tap water in the middle.

setup.art: A child with one hand in the warm bowl and one in the ice bowl, counting.
setup.caption: 2. One hand in each outside bowl for one minute.

setup.art: Both hands in the middle bowl, the child looking puzzled.
setup.caption: 3. Both hands in the middle. What does each hand say?

flow.do: 1. Set out the three bowls: warm water on the left, ice water on the right, tap water in the middle. 2. Ask your child to put one hand in each outside bowl. 3. Count slowly to 60.
flow.say: Put your left hand in the warm bowl and your right hand in the ice bowl. Keep them there while I count to 60.
flow.kid: Left hand in the warm bowl. Right hand in the ice bowl. Count to 60.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two-Hands Bowl. You get your hands warm and cold before the test.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to move both hands into the middle bowl at the same time. 2. Ask what each hand feels.
flow.say: Now put both hands in the middle bowl. Is this water warm or cold? Ask each hand.
flow.kid: Both hands in the middle bowl. Warm or cold? What does each hand say?

ask.q: What does each hand tell you?
good: The left hand says cold and the right hand says warm.

flow.parent: The hand from the warm bowl feels the water as cold. The hand from the ice bowl feels it as warm. Let your child enjoy the surprise before explaining.

flow.do: 1. Dry the hands. 2. Stand the thermometer in the middle bowl and wait until the line stops. 3. Read it together.
flow.say: Your hands disagree. Let's ask the thermometer. How many numbers does it give?
flow.kid: Read the thermometer in the middle bowl. One number or two?

check.q: Why did one hand feel the middle water as warm and the other as cold?
options: The water was warm on one side and cold on the other
Each hand felt whether it was getting warmer or cooler, and one hand was colder to start with
One hand is better at feeling than the other
check.why: The hand from the ice was cold, so it gained heat in the middle bowl and felt warm. The hand from the warm bowl lost heat and felt cold. The thermometer showed the water was one temperature. Picking 'warm on one side' is a sensible guess, and you can test it: swap hands, and the feelings swap too.

activities.title: The Temperature Hunt: measure five things at home

materials.item: a laboratory thermometer that reads from about minus 10 to 110 °C, or a digital kitchen probe thermometer. A fever thermometer will not work, because it reads only from about 32 to 42 °C.
a steel tumbler
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Never put a laboratory thermometer in your mouth or near the stove. Lay it flat when you are not holding it.

schedule.what: Guess, then measure: the room, the balcony or a window, tap water, fridge water, and water that stood out overnight.

activities.record: Make a table with three columns: the place, my guess, and what the thermometer read. Then put the five things in order from coldest to warmest.
activities.context: This activity is practice in reading a thermometer, by measuring five things around the home.

setup.art: A child holding a thermometer near a window in the shade, a notebook in the other hand.
setup.caption: 1. Guess first, then measure each place.

setup.art: A thermometer standing in a tumbler of water next to an open fridge door.
setup.caption: 2. Measure water from the tap and from the fridge.

flow.do: 1. List five things. They are room air, air at a shady window, tap water, fridge water, and water that stood out overnight. 2. Ask your child to guess a temperature for each.
flow.say: We are going to measure five things. Guess a number for each one first. Which will be the coldest? Which will be the warmest?
flow.kid: Five things to measure. Guess a number for each. Which is coldest?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Temperature Hunt. You guess the temperature of five things at home.

flow.do: 1. Measure each one. 2. For air, hold the thermometer by its top in the shade for 2 minutes. 3. For water, stand it in a tumbler for about a minute. 4. Write each number next to the guess.
flow.say: Wait until the line stops each time. How close was your guess?
flow.kid: Measure each one. Wait until the line stops. Write the number.
flow.parent: Keep the thermometer out of sunshine, because the Sun warms the thermometer itself and gives a reading that is too high. The overnight water should match the room within a degree or so. That is a good surprise to talk about.

flow.do: Ask which two numbers were closest, and why.
flow.say: The water that stood out all night read almost the same as the room. Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: The overnight water matched the room. Why?

check.q: A tumbler of water stood in the room all night. In the morning it reads the same as the room air. Why?
options: Water always reads the same as air
It had all night to share heat with the room, until both were the same
The thermometer is stuck
check.why: Things left together for a long time share heat until they are at the same temperature. Fridge water does not read the same as the air in your room, so 'water always reads the same' cannot be right.

activities.title: Make a Straw Thermometer

materials.item: a small glass bottle with a cap, such as an empty sauce or jam bottle. A small plastic water bottle also works.
a clear drinking straw
a small ball of atta dough, clay or plasticine, to seal round the straw
water with two drops of food colour or a pinch of haldi
two big bowls: one of hot water mixed by a grown-up, one of ice water
a marker pen
a laboratory thermometer that reads from about minus 10 to 110 °C, or a digital kitchen probe thermometer. A fever thermometer will not work, because it reads only from about 32 to 42 °C.

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the hole in the cap and mixes the hot water. Hold the bottle by its neck when it is in the hot bowl.

schedule.what: Make a bottle thermometer. Put it in hot water and in ice water, and mark where the coloured water reaches.

activities.record: Mark the straw at room temperature, in hot water and in ice water. Write the real thermometer's reading next to each mark.
activities.context: In this activity you build your own thermometer from a bottle and a straw, and watch the liquid climb.

setup.art: A small glass bottle filled to the brim with coloured water, a straw pushed through the cap and sealed with a ball of dough.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the bottle to the brim. Seal a straw in the cap.

setup.art: The bottle standing in a bowl of hot water, the coloured water risen high up the straw, with a marker line.
setup.caption: 2. Stand it in hot water. Watch the level climb.

setup.art: The bottle standing in a bowl of ice water, the coloured water low in the straw.
setup.caption: 3. Then in ice water. Watch it fall.

flow.do: 1. Make a hole in the cap just wide enough for the straw. 2. Fill the bottle to the very top with coloured water. 3. Push the straw through the cap so it goes about 3 cm into the water. 4. Screw on the cap and seal round the straw with dough. 5. The water should show a little way up the straw.
flow.say: We are making our own thermometer. The bottle is the bulb and the straw is the tube. The bottle must be full, with no air inside.
flow.kid: Fill the bottle right to the top. Seal the straw in the cap with dough.
flow.parent: If the water does not show in the straw, squeeze in a little more water through the straw with a dropper, or press the dough down. Air bubbles inside make it less clear, so fill right to the brim.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Straw Thermometer. You build a thermometer from a bottle, a straw and coloured water.

flow.do: Mark the level on the straw with the marker. Write 'room' and the real thermometer's room reading next to it.
flow.say: Let's mark where the water is now. What will happen to it in hot water? Why?
flow.kid: Mark the water level. Now guess: what will hot water do to it? Why?

flow.do: 1. Stand the bottle in the bowl of hot water. 2. Watch the straw for 5 minutes. 3. Mark the highest level, and write the hot water's real temperature beside it.
flow.say: Watch the straw closely. What is the coloured water doing?
flow.kid: Watch the straw. Is the water going up or down?
flow.parent: In the first few seconds the level may dip a little, because the glass warms and expands first. Then the water warms and climbs, often several centimetres. This is real and worth pointing out.

check.q: Why did the coloured water climb up the straw?
options: The hot water pushed in through the glass
The water in the bottle warmed, expanded and needed more space, so it went up the straw
Steam lifted it
check.why: Warm water takes up a little more space than cool water. The only place it can go is up the narrow straw, so a tiny bit of extra water makes a long rise. A real thermometer works the same way. The hot bowl water cannot get through the glass, so 'pushed in' cannot be the reason.

flow.do: 1. Move the bottle into the ice water. 2. Watch for 5 minutes. 3. Mark the lowest level.
flow.say: Now into the cold. What do you think will happen? Why?
flow.kid: Now put it in ice water. What happens to the level?
flow.parent: The level falls, often below the room mark. Your child now has a thermometer with three marks. A real thermometer was made the same way, with marks for ice and boiling water.

activities.title: Which Way Is the Heat Going? A home hunt

materials.item: a notebook and pencil, and coloured pencils

activities.safety: Look, do not touch, anything that might be hot, such as the stove, the iron or a pressure cooker.

schedule.what: Find six things at home that are warming up or cooling down. Draw each one with an arrow showing which way the heat goes.

activities.record: Draw six things. Add a red arrow for each, pointing from the warmer thing to the cooler thing.
activities.context: In this activity you hunt for things at home that are warming up or cooling down, and draw which way their heat moves.

setup.art: A kitchen with an idli steamer cooling on the stove, a bowl of curd out of the fridge, and a tumbler with ice, each with a small red arrow.
setup.caption: 1. Find things that are warming up or cooling down.

setup.art: A notebook page with six small drawings, each with a red arrow from warm to cool.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each one with a heat arrow.

flow.do: 1. Walk through the home together. 2. Find six things that are warming up or cooling down. 3. For each, ask which way the heat is going.
flow.say: Let's find things that are warming up or cooling down. For each one, where is the heat going? From what, into what?
flow.kid: Find six things getting warmer or cooler. Where is the heat going?
flow.parent: Good finds: a cooker cooling after cooking, curd warming on the table, ice melting in a drink, a hot iron cooling, a child's hand on a cold tile, clothes drying in the sun. For ice in a drink, the heat goes from the drink into the ice.
flow.context: This is the first step of the home hunt. You find things that are warming up or cooling down.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw each one with a red arrow from the warmer thing to the cooler thing.
flow.say: Draw each one. Make the heat arrow go from the warmer thing to the cooler thing.
flow.kid: Draw each one. Add a red heat arrow, from warm to cool.

check.q: Ice cubes are melting in a tumbler of lemon juice. Which way is the heat going?
options: From the ice into the juice
From the juice into the ice
No heat is moving
check.why: The juice is warmer than the ice, so heat moves from the juice into the ice. That is why the ice melts and the juice gets colder. Picking 'from the ice' is how it can feel, because the drink gets cold, but what really happens is that the juice loses heat.

projects.title: My Temperature Diary: seven days at the window

materials.item: a laboratory thermometer that reads from about minus 10 to 110 °C, or a digital kitchen probe thermometer. A fever thermometer will not work, because it reads only from about 32 to 42 °C.
a shady spot at a window or on a balcony, where the thermometer can hang or lie in the shade
a notebook with a table drawn in it, and a pencil

projects.safety: Keep the thermometer in the shade, tied or taped so it cannot fall from the window or balcony.

schedule.what: Choose a shady spot. Draw the diary table. Take the first morning and afternoon readings.
Read the thermometer at 8 in the morning and 2 in the afternoon.
Read at 8 in the morning and 2 in the afternoon.
Read at 8 in the morning and 2 in the afternoon.
Read at 8 in the morning and 2 in the afternoon.
Read at 8 in the morning and 2 in the afternoon.
Last readings. Draw a line graph and find the warmest and coolest times.

projects.record: A table with the day, the 8 am reading, the 2 pm reading and the weather in one word (sunny, cloudy, rainy). On day 7, a line graph with two lines.
projects.context: In this 7-day project you read a thermometer at the same place every morning and afternoon, and find the pattern.

setup.art: A thermometer taped to the shady side of a window grill, with a child reading it in the morning light.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the thermometer in the shade. Read it at 8 am.

setup.art: A notebook with a seven-day table and a line graph with two lines, one for morning and one for afternoon.
setup.caption: 2. Read again at 2 pm. On day 7, draw the graph.

flow.do: 1. Find a shady spot at a window or balcony. 2. Fix the thermometer there so it cannot fall. 3. Draw the table. 4. Take the first readings at 8 am and 2 pm.
flow.say: For seven days we will read the same thermometer at the same place, every morning and every afternoon. Which will be warmer, do you think? Why?
flow.kid: Read the thermometer at 8 in the morning and 2 in the afternoon. Which will be warmer? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Temperature Diary. You set up a thermometer in the shade and take the first readings.

flow.do: Each day, read at 8 am and 2 pm. Write the numbers and one word for the weather.
flow.say: Time for the reading. What does it say? Is it warmer or cooler than yesterday at this time?
flow.kid: Read the thermometer. Write the number. Write the weather.
flow.wait: Come back every day at 8 am and 2 pm, for six more days.
flow.parent: The afternoon is usually warmer, because the Sun has been heating the ground and the air all morning. On a rainy or very cloudy day the gap is often smaller. If you miss a reading, leave a gap. Do not guess a number.

flow.do: 1. On day 7, help your child draw a line graph. 2. Put the days along the bottom and temperature up the side. 3. Draw one line for 8 am and one for 2 pm.
flow.say: Let's draw your week. Which day had the biggest gap between morning and afternoon? What was the weather that day?
flow.kid: Draw your graph. Which day had the biggest gap? What was the weather?

check.q: Why is 2 in the afternoon usually warmer than 8 in the morning?
options: The Sun has been heating the ground and air for hours
The thermometer warms up by itself during the day
People cook lunch
check.why: From sunrise, sunlight heats the ground, the walls and the air. By the early afternoon they have taken in the most heat. At night the heat leaks away to the sky, so the morning is cooler. Lunch cooking warms a kitchen, but not the air outside a window.

challenges.title: Cool the Coffee Fast
challenges.problem: A tumbler of hot water is too hot to drink. Get it down to 40 °C as fast as you can, without a fridge, ice or adding cold water.
constraints: Start with one tumbler of hot water from a grown-up, all at the same temperature.
No fridge, no ice, and no adding water.
Measure with the thermometer and time it.
materials: two steel tumblers and a davara or a wide steel bowl
a laboratory thermometer that reads from about minus 10 to 110 °C, or a digital kitchen probe thermometer. A fever thermometer will not work, because it reads only from about 32 to 42 °C.
a plate, a spoon, a hand fan or a sheet of card
general: Pour the water between two tumblers, or a tumbler and a davara, again and again. Much more water touches the air, so heat leaves faster.
Pour it into a wide plate. A shallow layer has a big top for heat to leave through.
Fan it. Moving air carries warm air away from the water, so cooler air keeps touching it.
creative: Stand the tumbler in a bigger bowl of tap water, as in Tumbler in a Bowl.
Stir it with a cold steel spoon, and swap the spoon each minute.
Combine two ideas, such as pouring onto a plate and fanning.
challenges.your_turn: Try your best idea and time it. Then try a second idea. Which was faster, and why do you think so?

setup.art: A grown-up pouring water from a steel tumbler into a davara from a height, a long stream between them.
setup.caption: 1. Try pouring between a tumbler and a davara.

setup.art: Hot water spread in a wide steel plate, with a child fanning it with a sheet of card and a thermometer lying in it.
setup.caption: 2. Or spread it out and fan it. Time how long it takes to reach 40.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours one tumbler of hot water. 2. Read it. 3. Ask your child for ideas to cool it fast, with reasons.
flow.say: This water is too hot to drink. How can we get it down to 40 degrees quickly, with no fridge and no ice? Why would your idea work?
flow.kid: Cool this hot water to 40 degrees. No fridge. No ice. What will you try? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Cool the Coffee Fast, a design challenge to cool hot water quickly.

flow.do: 1. Try the first idea and time how long it takes to reach 40 °C. 2. Start again with fresh hot water at the same temperature. 3. Try a second idea and time it.
flow.say: Let's time your first idea. Now fresh water at the same temperature, and your second idea. Which was faster?
flow.kid: Time your first idea. Then try a second idea. Which was faster?
flow.parent: Pouring between two tumblers and spreading the water in a plate are usually the fastest. A grown-up should do the high pouring. Just leaving the tumbler alone can take 20 minutes or more.

flow.do: Ask why the fastest idea worked.
flow.say: Why did your fastest idea work so well? What did it change?
flow.kid: Why was your fastest idea the fastest?

check.q: Why does pouring coffee between a tumbler and a davara cool it quickly?
options: Pouring makes the coffee lose its heat to the air faster, because much more of it touches the air
The steel davara makes cold
Pouring shakes the heat out
check.why: Heat leaves through the surface that touches the cooler air. A falling stream and a wide davara give much more surface than a tall tumbler, so heat leaves faster. Some water also evaporates, which carries away heat too. Steel does not make cold.

challenges.title: Give Your Straw Thermometer Numbers
challenges.problem: Your straw thermometer goes up and down, but it has no numbers. Use the real thermometer to give it a scale, then use it to measure something new.
constraints: Use the straw thermometer from Make a Straw Thermometer.
You may use the real thermometer only to make the marks, not to check the final test until the end.
Your scale must have at least three numbered marks.
materials: a laboratory thermometer that reads from about minus 10 to 110 °C, or a digital kitchen probe thermometer. A fever thermometer will not work, because it reads only from about 32 to 42 °C.
bowls of water at three different temperatures, mixed by a grown-up
a strip of paper, cello tape and a pencil
general: Stand both thermometers in the same bowl. When both stop moving, mark the straw and write the real number.
Do this in three bowls: cool, room and warm. Then share the space between marks into equal steps.
creative: Tape a paper strip behind the straw and draw the scale on it.
Use a thinner straw to see if the marks spread further apart.
Test your thermometer on a fourth bowl, then check with the real one.
challenges.your_turn: Measure a new bowl of water with your straw thermometer. Write your reading. Then check it with the real thermometer. How close were you?

setup.art: The straw thermometer and a real thermometer standing together in a bowl of warm water, with a paper strip taped behind the straw.
setup.caption: 1. Put both thermometers in the same bowl. Mark the straw.

setup.art: A paper strip behind the straw with marks labelled 15, 30 and 45.
setup.caption: 2. Do three bowls. Draw a scale.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up mixes three bowls: cool, room and warm. 2. Stand both thermometers in the first bowl. 3. When both stop moving, mark the straw and write the real number. 4. Repeat for the other two bowls.
flow.say: We will copy the numbers from the real thermometer onto your straw. Wait until both stop moving before you mark it. Why must we wait?
flow.kid: Put both thermometers in one bowl. Wait. Mark the straw. Write the real number.
flow.parent: The straw thermometer is slow, because a whole bottle of water has to warm up. Give it 5 minutes in each bowl. This is a good chance to see why real thermometers have a small bulb.
flow.context: This is the first step of Give Your Straw Thermometer Numbers. You copy marks from a real thermometer onto your straw.

flow.do: 1. Tape a paper strip behind the straw. 2. Draw the three marks with their numbers. 3. Fill in steps between them.
flow.say: Now draw your scale. If 30 is here and 45 is here, where would 40 go?
flow.kid: Draw your scale on paper. Where would 40 go?

flow.do: Test a new bowl. Read the straw first, then check with the real thermometer.
flow.say: What does your straw thermometer say? Now let's check with the real one. How close were you?
flow.kid: Read your straw thermometer. Then check with the real one. How close?

check.q: Why does the straw thermometer take much longer to settle than a real thermometer?
options: Its bottle holds much more water, so it needs much more heat to warm up
Straws are lazy
The colour slows it down
check.why: A real thermometer has a tiny bulb, so very little heat warms it to the water's temperature. The bottle holds a lot of water, so it takes much longer to reach the same temperature. This is why real thermometers are thin.

videos.why: A short, clear cartoon from the old Eureka! series. It shows that temperature is how fast particles move, and heat is the energy that passes between things. Good for the parent, and for the child after the tumbler test.
