opts: How heavy something is
How hot or cold something is
How much heat something holds
quiz.why: A thermometer measures temperature: how hot or cold something is. It does not say how much heat a thing holds. A big bucket and a small cup can read the same.

quiz.p: Why must you wait before reading a thermometer in hot water?
opts: Heat takes time to move into the thermometer until it is as warm as the water
The numbers need time to appear
The water needs time to get hot
quiz.why: A thermometer shows its own temperature. It reads right only after heat has moved in and it is as warm as the water, which takes about a minute.

quiz.p: Ravi puts one hand in warm water and one in ice water for a minute. Then he puts both in tap water. Why does each hand feel something different?
opts: The tap water is warmer on one side
Each hand feels whether it is warming up or cooling down
Ravi's hands are different
quiz.why: The hand from the ice gains heat in the tap water and feels warm. The hand from the warm water loses heat and feels cold. A thermometer shows one number for the whole bowl.

quiz.p: Why does the red liquid in a thermometer climb when it gets warmer?
opts: The liquid expands and the only place to go is up the narrow tube
Heat is lighter than air, so it floats up
The glass squeezes it upwards
quiz.why: Warmer liquid takes up more space. The narrow tube turns a tiny bit of extra liquid into a long rise. Heat is not a thing that floats, so the second answer cannot be right.

quiz.p: A hot dosa is put on a cool steel plate. Which way does heat move?
opts: From the plate into the dosa
From the dosa into the plate
No heat moves
quiz.why: Heat moves from the warmer thing to the cooler thing. The dosa is hotter, so heat goes from the dosa into the plate, and the plate gets warm.

quiz.p: Two tumblers, one of hot water and one of fridge water, stand in a room at 30 °C for 3 hours. What will they read?
opts: The hot one 60 °C, the cold one 8 °C, the same as at the start
Both about 30 °C
The hot one 8 °C and the cold one 60 °C
quiz.why: Both share heat with the room until they are the same as the room. In your own test, both ended within a degree or two of the room.

quiz.p: In the Hot Tumbler, Cold Tumbler test, why did the cold water warm up?
opts: Heat moved into it from the warmer air and table
Cold moved out of it into the room
The thermometer warmed it
quiz.why: The air and the table were warmer than the fridge water, so heat moved into the water. Nothing called cold moves. The thermometer is far too small to warm a whole tumbler.

quiz.p: A small katori of water is at 70 °C. A big bucket of water is at 40 °C. Which statement is true?
opts: The katori is hotter, but the bucket holds more heat
The katori is hotter and holds more heat
They hold the same heat
quiz.why: Temperature says how hot, and the katori is hotter. But the bucket has so much more water that it holds far more heat. It would melt much more ice.

quiz.p: Equal amounts of water at 80 °C and 20 °C are mixed. About what will the mix read?
opts: About 50 °C
quiz.why: With equal amounts, the hot water cools by as much as the cold water warms, so they meet halfway. Halfway between 80 and 20 is 50. Mixing can never make water hotter than the hottest part.

quiz.p: In 1790, a flask of snow in front of a mirror made a thermometer across the room fall. What did Pierre Prévost show?
opts: Snow sends out rays of cold
The thermometer gave more heat to the snow than it got back
Mirrors make things cold
quiz.why: Prévost said everything sends out heat, and warmer things send out more. The thermometer lost more heat to the snow than it gained, so it cooled. Only heat was moving.

quiz.p: Why can't a fever thermometer measure water from the fridge?
opts: It reads only from about 32 to 42 °C
It only works in the mouth
Water breaks it
quiz.why: A fever thermometer is made for bodies, which change only a little, so its range is short. Fridge water is far below 32 °C, so it just shows 'Lo'.

quiz.p: A tumbler of water on a sunny sill reads 45 °C, but the air in the shade reads 33 °C. What is the best explanation?
opts: Sunlight is heating the water directly, so it is warmer than the air
Heat is flowing from the shady air into the water
The thermometer is broken
quiz.why: Sunlight brings heat straight to the water, so the water ends up warmer than the air around it. Heat cannot flow by itself from the cooler shady air into warmer water.

items.p: The tool we use to measure how hot or cold something is, is called a ____.
items.why: A thermometer measures temperature. Your hand can only tell you whether it is warming up or cooling down.

items.p: On the Celsius scale, pure water freezes at ____ degrees and boils at ____ degrees.
items.why: The Celsius scale was made by marking melting ice as 0 and boiling water as 100, and cutting the space between into 100 equal degrees.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3, dips a thermometer into hot water and reads it straight away. What is wrong with her reading?
opts: Nothing, a thermometer is right at once
It will be too low, because the thermometer has not warmed up to the water yet
It will be too high, because thermometers start hot
items.why: Heat takes about a minute to move into the thermometer's bulb. Until then the thermometer is cooler than the water, so it reads too low. A strong answer says: wait until the line stops moving.

items.p: Farhan wants to measure the water in the fridge. He has a fever thermometer and a laboratory thermometer. Which should he use?
opts: The fever thermometer, because it is digital
The laboratory thermometer, because a fever thermometer reads only from about 32 to 42 °C
Either one
items.why: Fridge water is about 4 to 8 °C, far below what a fever thermometer can read, so it would just show 'Lo'. A laboratory thermometer reads from about minus 10 to 110 °C.

items.p: When you hold an ice cube, cold moves from the ice into your hand.
items.why: False. Heat moves from your warmer hand into the ice. Your hand cools because it is losing heat, and the ice melts because it is gaining heat. Nothing called cold moves.

items.p: A tumbler of hot water and a tumbler of cold water left in the same room for 3 hours will read about the same.
items.why: True. Both share heat with the room until they reach room temperature. In the Hot Tumbler, Cold Tumbler test, both ended within a degree or two of the room.

items.p: Sort these. Is each thing gaining heat or losing heat?
items: curd just taken out of the fridge, on the table
a hot idli steamer after the stove is off
an ice cube in your hand
your hand holding an ice cube
a cold bottle of water on a sunny sill
hot rasam in a bowl on the table
items.a: see items
items.why: A thing gains heat when what is around it is warmer, and loses heat when what is around it is cooler. A strong sorter compares each thing with what touches it.

items.p: Match each thing to its usual temperature.
pairs: a room in Chennai in May
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Knowing a few real temperatures helps you judge any number you read. Your body is warmer than most rooms, and a fridge is just above freezing.

items.p: Put these steps for reading a thermometer in water in the right order.
items: Read the number where the line ends
Stand the bulb in the water
Wait until the line stops moving
a: Stand the bulb in the water
Wait until the line stops moving
Read the number where the line ends
items.why: The bulb must be in the water, stirring mixes the water so it is the same all through, and waiting lets heat move into the bulb. Only then is the number right.

items.p: Kavya puts one hand in warm water and one in ice water. Then she puts both in a bowl of tap water. What does she feel?
opts: Both hands feel the tap water as warm
The hand from the warm water feels it as cold, and the hand from the ice feels it as warm
Both hands feel the tap water as cold
items.why: The warm hand loses heat to the tap water and feels cold. The cold hand gains heat and feels warm. Your skin feels whether it is warming or cooling, so the same water feels different to each hand.

items.p: In the Hot Tumbler, Cold Tumbler test, the cold tumbler's number went up from 8 to 16 in 20 minutes. Where did its heat come from?
items.a: From the air and the table around it. They were at room temperature, which was warmer than the cold water, so heat moved from them into the water.
items.why: A strong answer names where the heat came from and says why it moved that way: from the warmer air and table to the cooler water.

items.p: Why does a thermometer have such a narrow tube?
items.a: The liquid expands only a tiny bit when it warms. In a narrow tube, that tiny bit of extra liquid makes a long line that is easy to see and read.
items.why: A strong answer says that the liquid expands only a little, and that the narrow tube makes that small change show up as a big rise.

items.p: Revathi says, 'Shut the door, the cold is coming in!' What is really happening when the door is open on a cold night?
items.a: Heat from the warm room is going out through the open door into the colder air outside. The room cools down because it is losing heat. No cold is coming in.
items.why: A strong answer says that heat is leaving, and uses the rule that heat moves from warmer to cooler.

items.p: Draw a tumbler of hot water on a table. Draw red arrows to show where its heat goes.
items.a: Red arrows go out of the water into the air above it, out through the sides into the air, and down into the table.
items.why: A strong drawing shows heat leaving in several directions, always from the hot water to the cooler things that touch it.
items.art: A blank box with a steel tumbler drawn on a table, with a little steam.

items.p: Label the parts of this thermometer: bulb, narrow tube, liquid, scale.
items.a: The bulb is the round end at the bottom. The narrow tube runs up from it. The red liquid fills the bulb and part of the tube. The scale is the numbers along the side.
items.why: The bulb holds most of the liquid and must touch what you measure. The liquid climbs the narrow tube, and the scale turns its height into a number.
items.art: A drawing of a laboratory thermometer with four blank label lines pointing to the bulb, the tube, the red liquid and the numbers.

items.p: In the Tumbler in a Bowl test, the hot tumbler started at 62 °C and the bowl water at 30 °C. Where did the two numbers stop?
opts: Both at 62 °C
Both at about 37 °C, nearer the bowl's start
Both at 30 °C
items.why: Heat moved from the tumbler into the bowl until both were the same. The bowl held three times as much water, so it went up only a little while the tumbler came down a lot. They met at about 37 °C.

items.p: Arjun mixes one katori of water at 70 °C with one katori of water at 20 °C. About what will the mix read?
opts: About 45 °C
items.why: With equal amounts, the hot water comes down as far as the cold water goes up, so they meet halfway. Halfway between 70 and 20 is 45. In a real test it reads a little less, because the tumbler takes some heat.

items.p: Which holds more heat: a small katori of water at 70 °C, or a big bucket of water at 40 °C?
opts: The katori, because it is hotter
The bucket, because it has so much more water
They hold the same
items.why: Temperature says how hot a thing is, not how much heat it holds. The bucket has many times more water, so it holds far more heat and can melt much more ice. The katori is hotter, so heat would flow from it into the bucket if they touched.

items.p: Heat can move by itself from a cooler thing to a warmer thing.
items.why: False. Heat moves by itself only from warmer to cooler. A fridge can move heat the other way, but only by using electricity to pump it, which is why the back of a fridge is warm.

items.p: When the liquid in a thermometer warms up, it takes up more space. This is called ____.
items.why: Most things expand when they warm. In a thermometer, the expanding liquid has nowhere to go but up the tube.

items.p: Three of these are things losing heat. Which one is gaining heat?
opts: A hot iron after it is switched off
Fresh chapatis cooling in a box
Ice cream melting in a bowl
A cup of tea left on the table
items.why: Ice cream is colder than the room, so heat moves into it and it melts. The iron, the chapatis and the tea are all warmer than the room, so they lose heat.

items.p: Your skin is about 33 °C. Sort these. Does heat move into your hand or out of your hand when you touch each one?
items: a steel plate from the fridge
a marble floor in the morning
items.a: see items
items.why: Compare each thing with your skin. Anything warmer than 33 °C gives heat to your hand. Anything cooler takes heat from it. A strong answer compares numbers, not just how things feel.

items.p: Lakshmi read her hot tumbler every 5 minutes. Put her readings in time order, from the first to the last.
items.why: A hot tumbler cools all the time, so the readings go down. They also go down by less each time, because the water gets closer to room temperature.

items.p: In the Hot Tumbler test, the hot water fell 6 degrees in the first 5 minutes, but only 3 degrees between 15 and 20 minutes. Why did it slow down?
items.a: At the start the water was much hotter than the room, so heat left fast. As it cooled, it was closer to room temperature, so the difference was smaller and heat left more slowly.
items.why: A strong answer links the speed of cooling to the difference between the water and the room: the bigger the difference, the faster heat moves.

items.p: Your straw thermometer's coloured water climbed when you stood it in hot water. Explain why, using the word 'expand'.
items.a: The water in the bottle warmed up and expanded, so it needed more space. The only place it could go was up the straw, so the level rose.
items.why: A strong answer says the bottle water warmed, expanded, and had only the straw to go into.

items.p: Selvi takes a bottle of water out of the fridge. After an hour, it is covered in drops. She thinks water leaked through the bottle. What would you tell her?
items.a: The drops came from the air, not from inside. The cold bottle cooled the damp air touching it, and the water in that air turned into drops. To check, wipe the bottle dry. More drops appear, but the water inside does not go down.
items.why: A strong answer says the drops come from the air cooled by the cold bottle, and suggests a way to check.

items.p: Draw a graph with time along the bottom and temperature up the side. Draw one line for a hot tumbler and one for a cold tumbler on the same table, for 3 hours. Draw the room temperature as a dotted line.
items.a: The hot line starts high and curves down, steeply at first and then more gently, flattening at the dotted line. The cold line starts low and curves up, flattening at the dotted line too.
items.why: A strong graph shows both lines curving towards the room line and levelling off there, faster at the start than near the end.

items.p: Three friends argue about why their hands feel cold after holding a steel tumbler of fridge water.

views.says: The tumbler is sending cold into my hand.
My hand is sending heat into the tumbler. My hand feels cold because it is losing heat.
It is the same thing. Saying cold goes in or heat goes out are two ways of saying it.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Use something from this unit as evidence. Then say what another friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer usually agrees with Meenakshi: a thermometer shows the hand cooling and the tumbler warming, and Prévost showed that only heat moves. It admits Farhan has a point, since both words describe the same change, but explains that scientists measure the heat, and cold is just less of it.
items.why: There is a real argument here. Farhan's view is not silly, and scientists in the 1790s argued about it. A strong answer gives evidence and is fair to another side.

items.p: Thangam's thermometer reads 31 °C in her room. She hangs it in the afternoon sun and it reads 45 °C. Is the air in the sun really 45 °C?
opts: Yes, the thermometer is always right
Probably not. The sunlight is heating the thermometer itself, so it reads hotter than the air
No, thermometers do not work outside
items.why: A thermometer shows its own temperature. Sunlight heats its glass and liquid directly, so it reads higher than the air. That is why weather stations keep thermometers in a shady box with slats.

items.p: Two things that touch keep passing heat until they are at the same ____.
items.why: Heat moves only when there is a temperature difference. When the temperatures are the same, it stops.

items.p: In 1790, Marc-Auguste Pictet put a flask of snow in front of a curved mirror. A thermometer in front of a second mirror, across the room, fell. What did Pierre Prévost say was happening?
opts: The snow was sending out rays of cold
The thermometer was sending heat to the snow, and getting less back than it gave
The mirrors were cold
items.why: Prévost said everything sends out heat all the time, and warmer things send out more. The thermometer was warmer than the snow, so it gave out more than it got back, and cooled. Many people at the time thought the snow sent out cold, which is why it was a real argument.

items.p: Dhanya mixes 1 katori of water at 60 °C with 2 katoris of water at 15 °C. About what will the mix read?
opts: About 37 °C, halfway
About 30 °C, nearer the cold
About 50 °C, nearer the hot
items.why: Think of three katoris sharing heat. The total of the three starting numbers is 60 + 15 + 15 = 90, and 90 shared by 3 is 30. There is more cold water, so the mix is nearer the cold number.

items.p: If you leave a tumbler of water on the table for a whole day, it can end up a little cooler than the room.
items.why: True. Water evaporating from the top carries away a little heat, so open water often settles a degree or so below the air. A strong answer names evaporation as the reason.

items.p: Your hot tumbler gave its heat to the room. Why didn't the room's thermometer go up?
items.a: The room has a huge amount of air, walls and furniture compared with one tumbler. The tumbler's heat was shared among all of it, so the room warmed by far too little to see on the thermometer.
items.why: A strong answer says that the heat spread into something much bigger, so the rise was too small to measure, and may mention the Tumbler in a Bowl test, where a smaller amount of water did show the rise.

items.p: A thermometer only ever tells you its own temperature. So how can it tell you the temperature of the water?
items.a: When the thermometer stands in the water, heat moves between them until they are at the same temperature. Then the thermometer's own temperature is the water's temperature, so its reading is the water's too.
items.why: A strong answer uses the rule that things that touch end up at the same temperature, and explains why you must wait.

items.p: A big pot of sambar stays hot much longer than a small bowl of it, even though both started at the same temperature. Why?
items.a: The big pot holds much more sambar, so it holds much more heat. Heat leaves through the surface, and the big pot has less surface for each spoonful of sambar inside. So it takes much longer to lose its heat.
items.why: A strong answer uses the difference between heat and temperature: same temperature, but the pot holds far more heat.

items.p: Many people think hot water freezes faster than cold water. This is called the Mpemba effect. Describe a fair test you could do at home to check it.
items.a: Use two identical steel cups with the same amount of water, one hot and one cold. Put them side by side in the freezer at the same time. Check every 10 minutes and write when each one is frozen solid. Repeat it three times, because one try can be a fluke.
items.why: A strong test changes only the starting temperature, keeps the cups, amounts and place the same, decides what 'frozen' means, and repeats the test. Scientists still argue about this effect, so either result is interesting.

items.p: A family is deciding how to keep their flat cooler in May, without an AC.

views.says: Close the windows and curtains in the day. The hot air outside can't heat the room as fast.
Open everything and let the breeze in. Moving air cools us down.
Close them while it is hotter outside than inside, and open them in the evening when outside is cooler.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Use what you know about heat moving from warmer to cooler. Then say what another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer usually backs Kavya: heat comes in when the outside is hotter, and goes out when the outside is cooler, so a thermometer inside and outside tells you when to open the windows. It admits Paati is right that a breeze cools our skin even when the air is warm, because it helps sweat evaporate, and Amma is right about the hottest hours.
items.why: This is a real choice families make, with a real trade-off. A strong answer uses the direction of heat flow as evidence and is fair to the other views.

items.p: Sort these sentences. Is each one about temperature or about amount of heat?
items: The big bucket melted more ice than the small katori.
The thermometer reads 30 in the room.

items.why: Temperature is a number for how hot something is. The amount of heat depends on how hot it is and how much of it there is. A strong sorter asks: is this about how hot, or about how much it can warm other things?

items.p: A fridge keeps its inside cold, but the back of the fridge is warm. Why?
opts: The fridge pumps heat out of its inside and lets it out at the back
The light inside is hot
Cold and heat are both made inside it
items.why: Heat does not move by itself from the cold inside to the warm kitchen. The fridge uses electricity to pump it out, and the heat leaves through the grille at the back. A fridge does not make cold. It moves heat.

items.p: Draw what the water particles might look like in a tumbler of cold water and in a tumbler of hot water. Show how they move.
items.a: Both drawings show many small dots packed close together. The cold ones have short wiggle lines. The hot ones have long wiggle lines, showing they jiggle faster.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the particles the same size and about the same distance apart, and shows the difference only in how fast they move, because that is what temperature is.
items.art: Two empty circles side by side, labelled 'cold water, zoomed in' and 'hot water, zoomed in'.

items.a: Hot water inside the tumbler, bowl water around it, the steel tumbler wall between them, and arrows pointing outwards from the hot water through the steel into the bowl water.
items.why: A strong label shows heat going one way only: from the hot water, through the steel, into the cooler water around it.

items.p: On the Celsius scale, anything colder than freezing water gets a ____ number, such as a freezer at about 18 below zero.
items.why: Zero is where water freezes, not where temperature ends. Colder than that, we count down below zero: minus 1, minus 2, and so on.

items.p: If temperature is how fast particles jiggle, could there be a coldest possible temperature? Explain your thinking.
items.a: Yes. If particles jiggle more slowly as things get colder, there must be a point where they are moving as little as they possibly can. Nothing could be colder than that. Scientists call it absolute zero, which is about minus 273 °C.
items.why: A strong answer reasons from the idea that temperature is jiggling: slower and slower must stop somewhere. Naming absolute zero is a bonus, not needed.

applications: Doctors and parents use clinical thermometers to check for fever.
Weather stations measure the air temperature in a shady box, so the Sun does not heat the thermometer itself.
Cooks use probe thermometers to check that milk is warm enough for curd, or that oil is hot enough for frying.
A fridge and an AC pump heat out of a room or a box, and let it out outside.
Railway tracks and concrete roads are laid with small gaps, so they have room to expand on hot days.
Hospitals keep vaccines between 2 and 8 °C, and check the temperature every day.
A pressure cooker cooks dal faster because the water inside boils at about 120 °C instead of 100 °C.
Engines have radiators that pass their heat into the air, so they do not overheat.

open_questions.q: Does hot water really freeze faster than cold water, and if so, why?
open_questions.why_open: Some careful experiments find it does, and others find it does not. Scientists still argue about whether the Mpemba effect is real and what causes it.

open_questions.q: Is the one-way spreading of heat the reason time only goes forwards?
open_questions.why_open: Heat always spreads from hot to cold, and never by itself the other way, just as time never runs backwards. Many physicists think the two are linked, but nobody is sure exactly how.

open_questions.q: How do our skin cells sense warmth and cold so precisely?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found special gates in nerve cells that open at certain temperatures. But how the brain turns their signals into the feeling of warmth is not fully understood.

maths.problem: Lakshmi read her hot tumbler every 5 minutes: 62, 56, 52, 48, 45 degrees. How many degrees did it fall in the first 5 minutes? And in the last 5 minutes? What do you notice?
maths.answer: 6 degrees in the first 5 minutes, and 3 degrees in the last 5 minutes. It cooled more slowly as it got closer to room temperature.
maths.explain: 62 minus 56 is 6. 48 minus 45 is 3. The falls in between were 4 and 4. So the falls get smaller: 6, 4, 4, 3. The water cools fastest when it is furthest from the room's temperature.
maths.context: This is about the Hot Tumbler, Cold Tumbler test, where you read a hot tumbler every 5 minutes.
maths.why_maths: Taking each reading from the one before shows how fast the water cooled, so you can see that it slows down.

maths.problem: In the same test, Lakshmi's room was 30 °C. Her hot tumbler started at 62 °C and her cold tumbler at 8 °C. How far was each tumbler from the room at the start? Which one would you expect to change faster at first?
maths.answer: The hot tumbler was 32 degrees above the room. The cold tumbler was 22 degrees below it. The hot one should change faster at first, because it was further from the room.
maths.explain: 62 minus 30 is 32. 30 minus 8 is 22. The bigger the difference, the faster heat moves. In her test the hot tumbler fell 6 degrees in the first 5 minutes, and the cold one rose 3.
maths.context: This is about the Hot Tumbler, Cold Tumbler test, where both tumblers stood in a room at 30 °C.
maths.why_maths: Finding each difference lets you predict which tumbler will change faster, before you look at the readings.

maths.problem: Arjun mixed 1 katori of water at 60 °C with 1 katori at 10 °C. What should the mix read? He measured 33 °C. Why might it be a little lower?
maths.answer: It should read about 35 °C. It was a little lower because some heat went into the steel tumbler and the air.
maths.explain: With equal amounts, the mix is halfway. 60 plus 10 is 70, and half of 70 is 35. Some of the hot water's heat warmed the tumbler and the air instead of the cold water, so the mix was 2 degrees lower.
maths.context: This is about the Half and Half experiment, where you mix hot and cold water.
maths.why_maths: Working out the halfway number gives a prediction, and the gap between the prediction and the real reading tells you that some heat went somewhere else.

maths.problem: A thermometer has a long line at every 10 degrees and a short line at every 2 degrees. The red liquid stops 3 short lines above the long line for 20. What does it read?
maths.explain: Each short line is 2 degrees. 3 short lines is 3 lots of 2, which is 6. 20 plus 6 is 26.
maths.context: This is about reading a laboratory thermometer, which has long lines for tens and short lines in between.
maths.why_maths: A thermometer is a number line standing up. Counting the small steps is how you read numbers between the labelled ones.

maths.problem: Selvi's Temperature Diary shows these 2 pm readings for a week in Bengaluru: 29, 30, 28, 24, 27, 29, 30 °C. On which day was it coolest? What might the weather have been that day? What was the difference between the warmest and coolest afternoon?
maths.answer: Day 4 was the coolest, at 24 °C. It was probably cloudy or rainy. The difference was 6 degrees, from 30 down to 24.
maths.explain: The smallest number is 24, on day 4. Clouds and rain stop sunlight heating the ground and air, so a rainy afternoon is cooler. 30 minus 24 is 6.
maths.context: This is about the Temperature Diary project, where you read a thermometer at the same place every afternoon for a week.
maths.why_maths: Finding the smallest number and the difference turns a list of readings into a pattern you can explain with the weather.

roots.context: We have measured hot and cold water, watched heat move, and found where things stop. Now we ask what heat moving tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your hot tumbler cooled and your cold tumbler warmed, until both read the same as the room. Nothing in the room was making cold. Heat moved out of the hot water, and from the air into the cold water. So cold is only less heat, and heat always moves from warmer to cooler.
deep_truth.habit: We talk about hot and cold as two opposite things that both flow, as in 'the cold is coming in'. But only heat ever moves. Cold is our name for having less of it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the hot and cold tumbler test, the hot water's temperature went down and the cold water's went up, and both stopped at room temperature. In the tumbler-in-a-bowl test, the water around the hot tumbler warmed while the tumbler cooled.

three.who_am_i: Your body is about 37 degrees, warmer than most rooms. So heat leaves you all day long, and the food you eat makes more.
three.what_is_life: A lizard on a wall basks in the morning sun to take in heat, because their body warms up from the world around them.
three.what_is_this_world: Left alone, a hot tumbler, a cold tumbler and a room all end up at one temperature. The Sun keeps making new warm places, and that is why the weather keeps changing.

roots.thread: In a room where everything is at one temperature, no heat moves. A difference is what makes heat move: a hot stove, a cold drink, a sunny wall. Heat moving makes winds blow, water evaporate and rain fall. So the many changes in the world start with differences, and each change is the world evening one of them out.

teachings.link: Heat does exactly this. It moves from the hotter thing to the cooler one until neither has more. Laozi wrote that people often do the opposite.

science.text: Heat moves by itself only from warmer to cooler. Scientists call this the second law of thermodynamics.
This one-way spreading of heat may be part of why time seems to go only forwards, never backwards. Physicists still argue about how the two are linked.

other_view.view: Heat spreading out is just countless particles bumping at random. Fast ones pass movement to slow ones simply because there are more ways for movement to be shared out than kept in one place. Calling it 'evening out' or 'giving to what has too little' is a nice picture, but nature has no aim to balance anything.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. Choices made: a fever thermometer cannot be used, because it reads only from about 32 to 42 °C, so one laboratory thermometer or digital probe is the single bought item, used in every part. Hot water is always half boiled and half tap water, about 60 to 65 °C, poured by a grown-up. With one thermometer, two tumblers can both be read in each 5-minute gap. A 150 ml tumbler of hot water in a 30 °C room cools only to about 45 °C in 20 minutes, so the experiment has a last reading after 3 hours, when both tumblers are within a degree or two of the room. The parent is told the hot tumbler may settle a little below the room because of evaporation. The Tumbler in a Bowl test uses about three times as much bowl water as tumbler water, so the two meet at about 37 °C within 15 to 20 minutes. The straw thermometer must be filled to the brim, and its level may dip for a few seconds before it climbs, so the step says so. The Temperature Diary keeps the thermometer in shade and tied down. No step needs a garden, a park or any animal. The spine is the Two-Hands Bowl, the Hot Tumbler test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1790, Marc-Auguste Pictet, a scientist in Geneva in Switzerland, set up two curved metal mirrors facing each other across a room. In front of one mirror he put a thermometer. In front of the other he put something hot. The thermometer rose, though nothing touched it. The mirrors were bouncing the heat across the room. Then Pictet put a flask of snow where the hot thing had been. The thermometer fell. It looked as if the snow was sending out rays of cold, and the mirrors were carrying them. Some scientists thought cold might be a real thing that travels, just like heat. In 1791, Pierre Prévost, another scientist in Geneva, explained it differently. Everything sends out heat all the time, he said, and warmer things send out more. The thermometer was sending heat to the snow and getting less back than it gave. So the thermometer cooled. Scientists today agree with Prévost. Cold is not a thing that moves. Only heat moves, and a cold thing is one that has less of it.
how_we_found_out.who: Marc-Auguste Pictet and Pierre Prévost, scientists in Geneva
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: When snow in front of a mirror made a distant thermometer fall, it seemed that cold was a thing that could travel. Prévost showed that the thermometer was simply losing more heat to the snow than it got back.
